title: Tenor saxophonist Eddie Loven
summary: He praises Eddie Loven, a warm-toned Detroit tenor who died at 24 without recording, and Julius Watkins.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Before I get any further, there's one guy I want to mention. Because this guy was so spectacular, I don't think I've ever heard anybody play a saxophone more personable than he did. He sounded like he was inside of his instrument. I rehearsed with him a few times at a club called The Twelve Horsemen, over on Jonorra(?) Street. And this guy had the warmest feeling! You could just feel it, you know, like there was heat coming off his instrument when he played. His name was Eddie Loven(?). And some years later, he went with Andy Kirk's orchestra. He died at 24 from tuberculosis. And Howard McGhee told me that Eddie Loven, at that time, when he died, he was as good as anybody playing a tenor saxophone, if he wasn't the best. And he never made a record! -- which is really kind of sad. You know, the guy never made a record. So I have to mention Eddie Loven(?), because he was really something special.
Yeah, he was a native of Detroit.
And that was the only place you heard him.
Yeah. The only place I heard of him playing, you know. Also Julius Watkins, the French horn player, he came up around that same period.
